excerpts.title: Build Flipper Phone App
excerpts.text: # PROJECT: APEX The Universal Electronic Intelligence Platform I think there's a much bigger product here than a Flipper Zero clone. **We should build a modular platform that can understand, communicate with, diagnose and operate an extraordinary range of electronic devices, using a smartphone as its control centre.** Not just NFC. Not just radio. Vehicles, smart buildings, wireless equipment, embedded electronics, industrial sensors, robotics, off-grid communications and eventually AI-assisted hardware analysis. I've started examining the open-source ecosystem, and several projects already demonstrate important parts of what we want. We can bring their ideas and compatible components together rather than reinventing everything. ## 1\. The vision  Visual direction: smartphone command centre plus expandable electronics modules. Think of APEX as three connected products. **APEX Mobile** Your command centre. Device discovery, diagnostics, visualisation, saved signals, workflows, AI interpretation and compatible-device controls. --- **APEX Core** A compact accessory with radios, NFC/RFID, infrared, GPIO and expansion ports. No expensive screen required because the phone provides it. --- **APEX Intelligence** An AI layer that helps identify equipment, explain signals, diagnose faults, connect protocols and create safe automation workflows. APEX is a working name, not a final brand. ## 2\. The open-source projects worth studying These are real projects I found, not hypothetical components.  **Flipper Zero firmware** (Foundation) Official firmware, applications and protocols. We can study its device abstractions, file formats and app ecosystem.  ---  **Bruce Firmware** An ESP32-based multitool supporting various combinations of Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Sub-GHz, infrared and RFID. Its modular hardware approach is especially relevant to our accessory.   ---  **HackRF One and Mayhem Mobile** Wideband software-defined radio research. There's already an Android project operating HackRF hardware directly over USB and processing radio samples on the phone. This validates an important part of our architecture.  ·   ---  **Proxmark3 and ChameleonUltra** Specialised RFID/NFC research hardware. Useful for understanding protocols, tag compatibility, reader behaviour and legitimate access-control testing.  ·   ---  **Meshtastic** Long-range, low-power mesh communication without mobile or internet coverage. A natural extension for remote sensors, field teams and off-grid equipment.   Other worthwhile projects include  for Android SDR visualisation,  for vehicle/industrial communication, and  for building our own accessory firmware.  This is an initial ecosystem survey, not yet a source-code audit or proof that these projects can be merged directly. ## 3\. The full capability roadmap I'd organise the product into 12 engineering modules, rather than building a collection of unrelated hacking utilities. Explore the proposed capability register (modules) - All - Core - Advanced - Research Current selection unavailable. The platform should deliberately distinguish between passive observation, authenticated control, laboratory simulation and transmit-capable testing. That protects users and makes the product suitable for professional diagnostics rather than unreliable claims about universal access. ## 4\. Hardware strategy: One brain, many modules The clever approach is not to cram everything into one circuit board immediately. **Android / iOS Command Centre** Display • AI • Storage • Processing **APEX Core** ESP32-S3 controller • USB-C • BLE • Secure firmware Each accessory would report its supported capabilities to the app. That means we could add better radios, additional antennas and new interfaces over time without redesigning the entire software platform. For early development, I'd use existing development boards. Custom circuit-board design should come only after the protocol, power and reliability tests succeed. ## 5\. The AI layer could become the differentiator Consider three practical scenarios. **Scenario A: An unknown wireless sensor** You have a wireless temperature sensor in front of you. APEX scans with supported hardware, records transmissions, identifies likely modulation and protocol formats, and explains what the captured data may represent. It could suggest an appropriate decoder and build a local device profile. **Scenario B: Diagnosing an electronic device** You point your phone camera at a circuit board. APEX identifies visible components, retrieves likely datasheets and guides you through voltage or serial-interface tests using a connected instrument. **Scenario C: Working on a vehicle** You connect a supported OBD-II adapter to your own vehicle. APEX reads diagnostic trouble codes, correlates supported sensor data, explains possible faults and produces a workshop report. Any security-sensitive or safety-critical controls remain outside ordinary diagnostic workflows. These are useful capabilities that could become commercially valuable, without relying on the ability to bypass protections. ## 6\. How I'd actually build it | Stage | Deliverable | Completion evidence | |--------|--------|--------| | 0\. Research | Source inventory, licensing audit, hardware feasibility matrix, PRD | Every capability classified and traced to a supported technology | | 1\. App foundation | Android application, native bridges, device registry | Builds on a physical Android phone | | 2\. Hardware bridge | ESP32 firmware, authenticated USB/BLE protocol | Stable device connection, reconnection and telemetry | | 3\. Core functions | NFC, BLE, infrared and Sub-GHz modules | Real captures and tests on owned equipment | | 4\. Spectrum lab | Supported SDR hardware integration | Live FFT, waterfall and sample export | | 5\. Professional tools | Electronics, vehicle and IoT diagnostics | Reproducible tests against controlled fixtures | | 6\. Intelligence | Local/optional cloud AI, protocol helpers, reporting | Evaluated identification accuracy and clear uncertainty | | 7\. Productisation | Modular accessory PCB, documentation, security review | Prototype validation and compliance testing | I'd put the code in a monorepo with separate `apps/mobile`, `firmware/core`, `packages/protocol`, `packages/device-drivers`, `packages/intelligence`, `hardware` and `docs` directories. **Important licensing decision\:** we should study GPL projects as references, but not indiscriminately paste their code into a proprietary product. Maintain a provenance and licensing register from the first commit. ## 7\. Where we can take it commercially The greatest opportunity isn't necessarily a gadget sold to hobbyists. We could have a free mobile toolkit, a paid professional diagnostics suite, specialised accessory modules and enterprise versions for equipment maintenance, facilities management and electronics laboratories. The long-term moat would be the device compatibility database, robust drivers, workflow engine and trustworthy AI diagnostics, not merely a collection of radio chips. ## What I would do next I would treat the initial research as a starting point and prepare a **full engineering PRD and repository intake plan**, including the approximately 12 capability areas above, exact open-source dependencies, hardware requirements, test fixtures, licensing and implementation sequence. And I would make one architectural decision now: **APEX should be a platform that can support many different instruments, including existing Flipper Zero hardware, rather than depending on one custom device.** That gives us a real path from a phone-only application to a powerful modular electronics platform. The project remains at the research and architecture stage. No app, prototype hardware or implementation repository has been created yet.

excerpts.title: Build Flipper Phone App
excerpts.text: A Flipper Zero-style app on your phone could turn it into a **portable electronics toolkit, wireless signal analyser, universal remote, device controller and security-testing platform**\. You could use it to discover devices around you, communicate with electronics, analyse signals, control your own equipment and automate certain tasks. The interesting part is that a smartphone has a much more powerful processor, touchscreen, camera, internet connection and AI capabilities than a Flipper Zero. We could use those to build something that goes well beyond the original. ## 1\. What it could actually do  **NFC and RFID tools** Read compatible NFC tags, inspect tag information, write supported tags, manage your own NFC automations and test authorised access-control equipment. Some RFID standards and secure access credentials require specialised external hardware. ---  **Radio signal explorer** With an external CC1101 module, receive and analyse compatible Sub-GHz signals from your own wireless sensors, doorbells, weather stations and remotes. Transmit supported signals on authorised frequencies, subject to radio regulations. ---  **Universal infrared remote** Control compatible TVs, projectors, air conditioners, LED lighting and other infrared equipment. Create custom remote layouts and sequences. Requires a built-in IR blaster or a compatible accessory. ---  **Bluetooth and electronics** Discover nearby BLE devices, inspect advertised services, communicate with compatible peripherals, read sensor measurements and control your own ESP32 or Arduino projects. ---  **Wi-Fi and network diagnostics** Inspect available network information, diagnose connection quality, identify devices on networks you administer and troubleshoot connected equipment. Deeper Wi-Fi packet capture and monitor-mode features need compatible external hardware. ---  **Hardware and circuit diagnostics** Use an external microcontroller as a GPIO controller, UART console or I²C/SPI interface. Diagnose embedded equipment, test sensors and inspect serial communication. ## 2\. What we could add that a Flipper Zero doesn't normally offer This is where the phone-based approach becomes much more interesting. | Advanced feature | What it would do | |--------|--------| | **AI signal assistant** | Explain captured signals, identify likely protocols and suggest safe diagnostic tests | | **Visual device map** | Display discovered BLE, Wi-Fi and connected devices, with signal-strength information | | **Smart home command centre** | Combine IR, supported local APIs and radio controls for your own appliances | | **Automation engine** | Run actions when an authorised NFC tag is scanned or a known BLE device connects | | **Device inventory** | Maintain a searchable catalogue of sensors, remotes, tags and hardware | | **AI electronics technician** | Use the phone camera to inspect circuit boards and help troubleshoot components | | **Portable cybersecurity laboratory** | Run permission-based assessments of supported wireless devices and protocols | ## 3\. Three versions we could build **Version A: App only** NFC, Bluetooth, supported Wi-Fi diagnostics, automations and AI assistance. No hardware purchases, although capabilities vary by phone. --- **Version B: App + mini accessory** Everything above, plus infrared, compatible Sub-GHz communications, 125 kHz RFID and hardware debugging. This is the closest equivalent to a Flipper Zero. --- **Version C: AI-powered electronics and security platform** Everything from A and B, with advanced diagnostics, device management, extensible tools and intelligent workflows. More ambitious, but technically achievable in stages. ## 4\. What it wouldn't automatically be able to do It wouldn't be a magic device that opens every door, starts any car or controls every wireless product. Modern encrypted access systems, rolling-code remotes and secure credentials cannot simply be copied and replayed. A phone also cannot transmit arbitrary radio signals merely because software requests it. These are genuine hardware and security limitations.  **My preferred direction is Version C, built incrementally.** Start with an app-only Android release, then add the compact hardware accessory and AI features. The bigger opportunity is to make a sophisticated wireless and electronics toolkit accessible to anyone with a smartphone, rather than requiring everyone to buy a dedicated device.

excerpts.text: **Yes. We could build a Flipper Zero-style app that runs directly on a smartphone, using the phone's existing hardware wherever possible and inexpensive external modules for the remaining capabilities.** And there's an interesting opportunity here: instead of reproducing the Flipper Zero exactly, we could build something more capable, with a modern touchscreen interface, better storage, automation and expandable hardware. ## What I found in your GitHub repository I inspected , including its firmware, hardware documentation and licence. It's a genuine embedded-hardware project, not simply a mobile app. It uses a modified version of the Flipper firmware and substitutes cheaper components. The MK1 design includes\: - **STM32WB55** microcontroller, the device's main processor. - **CC1101** radio module for Sub-GHz communications. - **ST25R3916** for NFC. - **Infrared transmitter and receiver**\. - **SPI/UART/GPIO** for connecting additional electronics. - An LCD, buttons and SD card. The author reports working Sub-GHz and NFC functionality, although some external drivers remain unfinished. The MK1 also lacks 125 kHz RFID. Most importantly, this software is written for the STM32 microcontroller and its attached electronics. **We cannot simply install that firmware on an iPhone or Android device.** We would need to port or reimplement its capabilities using mobile operating-system APIs. ## What could the app actually do? | Flipper capability | Phone alone | External hardware | |--------|--------|--------| | NFC tag reading | Yes, supported tag types | For more advanced protocols | | NFC tag emulation | Limited, mainly Android | For broader compatibility | | Bluetooth LE scanning | Yes | No | | Wi-Fi discovery | Yes, with OS restrictions | For advanced radio diagnostics | | Infrared remote controls | Only phones with IR blasters | USB-C/Bluetooth IR module | | Sub-GHz signals | No | CC1101 transceiver | | 125 kHz RFID | No | RFID reader module | | iButton / 1-Wire | No | Adapter | | GPIO / hardware control | No general-purpose GPIO | ESP32 or other controller | The major distinction is between Android and iOS. Android offers substantially more flexibility for native NFC, USB devices and supported radio operations. iOS has tighter restrictions. **I'd build Android first, then bring the supported features to iPhone.** ## The architecture I would build **FLIPPER-STYLE MOBILE APP** Android first, iOS where supported NFC • Bluetooth • Wi-Fi • IR • Sub-GHz • Automation Native mobile APIs + device communication protocol **Phone hardware** Built-in NFC, BLE and Wi-Fi **Pocket module** ESP32 + CC1101 + IR + RFID **Local signal library** Saved captures, device profiles, diagnostics and authorised test workflows I'd use React Native with Expo development builds for the interface, native Kotlin modules for Android hardware access, and C/C++ firmware for an optional ESP32-based accessory. We could use Flutter instead, but React Native fits your existing development approach. The optional accessory could be tiny, without a screen or buttons, because the phone already supplies those. ## What the app might look like **POCKET LAB** (Connected) DEVICE STATUS ## Ready to explore. 3 native interfaces available NFC • Bluetooth • Wi-Fi NFC Tools Read compatible tags Bluetooth Discover BLE devices Sub-GHz External radio module Infrared Remote control library Wi-Fi Network diagnostics My Signals Saved device profiles Concept interface, not a working app ## The development plan 1. **Phase 1: Phone-only app.** NFC reader, BLE explorer, Wi-Fi diagnostics, signal library and a clean interface. 2. **Phase 2: External hardware.** Add CC1101, infrared and RFID capabilities through a compact, inexpensive USB-C or BLE accessory. 3. **Phase 3: Advanced functions.** Signal visualisation, protocol analysis, scripts, automation and a plugin architecture for authorised security testing. 4. **Phase 4: Cross-platform.** Port supported functionality to iOS while retaining Android's more capable hardware integration. There is one important licensing consideration: the repository contains GPLv3-licensed firmware. If we incorporate its GPL-covered code into our distributed software, we need to comply with the corresponding source-sharing obligations. A separately implemented mobile app communicating with independently licensed accessory firmware may give us more flexibility. ## My recommendation Don't try to run the original firmware inside a phone emulator as the main solution. That would reproduce the user interface without providing the missing radio hardware. Instead, **make the phone the Flipper's brain and touchscreen, and make the external hardware optional**\. We could end up with a system that provides many of the same legitimate electronics and security-testing functions, without requiring users to buy a complete Flipper Zero. One question that affects the hardware strategy: **do you want this to work entirely on the phone, or are you happy with a tiny USB-C/Bluetooth accessory to unlock the full set of features?**
